review:
Leap of Fate is a fast-moving action roguelite from Clever Plays that blends cyberpunk style, supernatural themes, and intense twin-stick combat into a challenging experience centered around growth through repetition and mastery. Rather than focusing heavily on lengthy storytelling or traditional progression systems, the game builds its identity around speed, adaptability, and repeated attempts at conquering a dangerous mystical trial. The result is a stylish action title that combines futuristic technology and arcane powers in a world that feels both unusual and memorable.

The setting presents a version of New York transformed by hidden magic and advanced technology existing side by side. Powerful individuals known as technomages operate within this dangerous world, balancing supernatural abilities with technological advancement. Players take control of one of four unique characters who must survive a brutal supernatural challenge known as the Crucible of Fates. This trial serves as both a test of skill and a deeply personal journey where participants confront fears, regrets, and internal struggles while pursuing power and understanding.

Each playable character introduces meaningful differences that go beyond visual appearance. Their backgrounds shape both narrative themes and combat mechanics, creating distinct approaches to gameplay. One character may focus on mobility and precision while another emphasizes raw destructive power or tactical control. Because every character plays differently, switching between them significantly changes how players approach encounters and progression.

Combat becomes the heart of the experience almost immediately. Leap of Fate demands quick thinking and sharp reflexes, placing players in arenas filled with dangerous enemies and relentless attacks. Movement is constant. Standing still rarely leads to survival. Dodging incoming threats, repositioning carefully, and chaining abilities together become essential skills rather than optional strategies. The combat system rewards precision and awareness while maintaining an aggressive pace that keeps encounters exciting.

A defining mechanic comes through movement abilities that allow players to rapidly traverse battlefields while avoiding danger. These systems create a combat flow built around mobility and positioning rather than simply absorbing damage or overwhelming enemies with brute force. Encounters become a balance between offense and survival where even small mistakes can carry major consequences.

The roguelite structure reinforces this intensity. Death sends players back to earlier stages, but failure rarely feels meaningless. Progression systems provide permanent improvements and unlocks that slowly strengthen future attempts. This creates a satisfying loop where every defeat contributes toward eventual success. Learning enemy behavior, improving reaction speed, and understanding ability combinations become equally important forms of progression.

Randomization also plays an important role in maintaining replay value. Enemy placement, upgrade opportunities, and progression paths shift between runs, forcing players to adapt rather than relying entirely on memorized strategies. No single build guarantees victory every time. Flexibility becomes critical, encouraging experimentation with different abilities and upgrades.

Character development systems add another layer of strategic depth. Players unlock magical powers, passive enhancements, and combat modifiers that dramatically influence playstyle possibilities. Some combinations emphasize survivability while others create opportunities for devastating offensive builds. Experimenting with different upgrades becomes part of the long-term appeal, especially as players discover powerful synergies capable of transforming combat approaches.

Enemy variety strengthens the overall gameplay loop. Different threats require adjustments in positioning and ability usage, preventing combat from becoming repetitive despite repeated runs. Stronger opponents introduce escalating challenges that continually push players toward better execution and stronger decision-making. The difficulty remains demanding throughout much of the experience, rewarding persistence and improvement rather than simple luck.

Visually, Leap of Fate creates a compelling atmosphere through its fusion of cyberpunk environments and supernatural imagery. Neon lighting, hidden magical organizations, futuristic architecture, and mysterious mystical elements combine to establish a setting that feels distinctive without relying on photorealistic presentation. The visual identity remains stylish and consistent while supporting the fast-paced gameplay.

Audio design complements combat effectively. Sound effects provide satisfying feedback during encounters while music reinforces tension and momentum during more difficult battles. Together, the presentation creates an atmosphere that supports both the futuristic setting and supernatural themes.

The narrative takes a lighter approach compared to heavily story-driven games. Character arcs and world-building exist primarily to support gameplay progression rather than dominate the experience. While players seeking extensive storytelling may desire more depth, the focused structure allows gameplay systems to remain the primary attraction.

Leap of Fate succeeds because it understands what it wants to deliver. Clever Plays built an experience focused on repetition, improvement, and mastery without unnecessary distractions. The combination of procedural progression, fast combat, and distinctive world design creates a gameplay loop that remains engaging across multiple sessions.

Players who enjoy roguelites built around skill development and replayability will likely find plenty to appreciate. The game does not always offer easy victories, but overcoming its challenges creates a satisfying sense of accomplishment that reinforces its strongest qualities. While its difficulty and repetitive structure may not appeal to everyone, those willing to embrace its demanding nature will discover a rewarding action experience filled with style and intensity.

Really nice little Indie game

Still holds up tbh. Simple, fun, runs have good development but don't overstay their welcome, cool environments/themes. I don't want to oversell it - it's not a genre-defining game by any stretch, but it's very good if you don't mind the dated graphics. Speaking of which, the visuals really aren't much to look at by today's standards (or even when it came out, really) but the art style is nice, the voice acting isn't cheesy, and the game doesn't take itself too seriously which leads to it just being... fun. Something a lot of "modern games" seem to struggle with.

An action roguelike differentiated by a few unique mechanics (dash that teleports towards the mouse coursor, the ability to go back to stages you cleared to pick up the rewards you couldn't, such as heals), very tight, claustrophobic stages, high tempo, limited dashes/special attacks and an interesting, modern-occult-punk theme which is quite intriguing. If you're either an action roguelike fan or enjoy a setting and theme somewhere between Mage: the Ascension, EYE: Divine Cybermancy, Shadowrun and Secret World (with the caveat that there's not that much setting *material*, mostly vibes and snippets), I think you'll enjoy it!

[h1] Достаточно проходной проект. [/h1]

[h3] Геймплей [/h3]
Чувствуется достаточно однообразным. Да, глифы чуть-чуть разнообразят игру, но в основном уровни одни и те-же - ты бегаешь одно время против кучи хилых врагов(или расправляешься с ними скиллом, который предназначен для зачистки больших групп), а потом добиваешь чуть сильных противников. Эту беготню пытаются разбавить врагами, которые могут заграждать тебе путь, чтобы ты применяли свой дэш, но не больше.
Единственное, что здесь является особенным, это не самый обычный колдаун на способностях, а их определённное количество. Условно, на уровень у тебя может быть 3 дэша и 3 глифа, что тоже совсем немножко разнообразит игру. Но это скорее костыль, а не реально проработанная механика, потому что в игре есть ситуации, когда тебе нужно прожать один и тот же скилл дважды, пока ты бегаешь по уровню. А если стояло бы обычное кд, то персонажа можно было бы быстро убить.
Но и это выходит боком, потому что персонаж моментами может быть не особо поворотлив и спокойно ловить маслину, из-за чего не всегда получается уворачиваться. А дэш, напоминаю, ограничен в использовании. Хотя и эту ситуацию спасает то, что в игре достаточно хорошо отсыпают доп энергией и здоровьем, благодаря чему в критический момент вы всё таки сможете использовать уворот или любой другой с кил. Но в тот же критический момент эта неповоротливость сыграет не в вашу пользу.

[h3] Сеттинг [/h3]
Он странный. Как буд-то не туда не сюда - не в эзотерику, не в киберпанк. Нечего сказать больше.

[h3] Сюжет [/h3]
Ну и сюжетные линии героев... Я считаю важным про это сказать, потому что разработчики на странице игры утверждают, что он [i] ГлУбОкИй [/i]. Хотя на деле в игре почти нет сюжета. Максимум катсцена в начале игры, и катсцены в меню. На этом сюжет кончается. Максимум вы можете посмотреть одну из нескольких катсцен концовок, которые открываются при одном выполнении нужного для каждого ролика задания. Но это тоже выглядит просто как костыль.

Не рекомендую проект к покупке. Спокойно можно купить любой другой рогалик-шутер с видом сверху. Будет ощущаться более интересно.

P.S. Ну и от меня: [spoiler] Какая карточная система? Чуваки, вам просто вместо данжа с обычными локациями показали стол с картами, где ты абсолютнго так-же можешь куда-то пойти, а куда-то не пойти, и в от этого дуреете. Это буквально почти ни чем не отличается - ты лишь просто немного быстрее возвращаешься на локации, где ты оставил какой-то сундук и хочешь снова открыть или приходишь в магазин. Хотя в том же ETG ты можешь спокойно телепортироваться между комнатами, что почти никак не выделяет Leap of Fate в этом плане. [/spoiler]

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

I played this game on and off through the years but never for long, because plainly, it isn't much fun.
And I think the crux of 'not much fun' lies in the way dash/shadow walk works, i.e. very limited amount of dashes allowed (how much - varies per character) and while these dashes regenerate each combat, once you run out in the combat you can only rely on a randomly dropped resource, and if you didn't collect any, you are sheer out of luck.

Dashes are important because you are often put into a very tiny map with a loads and loads of enemies spawning from all directions in each wave, and past level 1 all them either faster than you, bigger than you (so they can box you into a corner if you aren't careful) or shoot farther than you - less limited dash would have helped to get out of situation stacked against you from the start, but no, it can only be used a few times. Doesn't help that dash is executed into the direction you are facing (and not in the direction you are currently moving), which means that often you dash right into a centre of the horde; there is an update tree which allows for it to become a dive bomb but because update trees are fully randomized, you might not get those abilities until much later if at all. 

Updates are fully randomized. The game uses card-based layout, similar to "Hand of Fate", but not only update cards random, each of them might be only updating one or two of the three types of skills (passive, mobility or active) and you'd never know which update you'd luck upon on this level, so any tactical build-building is out of window. Update cards also only allow to update one single skill even if you have souls/health to spare, which is again, not very fun and feels very limiting for no reason. Skill trees are also randomized upon each death, so it is randomized skill tree on top of randomized update card on top of randomized layout. 

People compared it to shmop - I don't know about that, but I 100% know that playing aggressive in this game is near impossible, and all I could do is backpedal and shoot backwards, like in a bad Serious Sam-like game; again, given that enemies come from all directions, and on tiny maps, the constant kiting is not fun. 

Layout is in cards and there are total of 6 stages each ending in Guardian (a boss). Actually I like card layout idea because you can always revisit the previously beaten card (as long as you stay on the same stage), game graciously highlights unopened chests or leftover health, so there is some strategy in how to progress through the layout, rudimentary it might be. 

You progress is wiped out on defeat - there is an (costly) option to continue, but even if you have enough currency to do so, you can again, only use it once, which is needlessly stingy. Permanent unlocks for each character happen from fulfilling a 'mission' - a random, overarching challenge which could be, for example, survive three combat cards on level 2 or update 8 skills before level 3 (and remember, update cards are entirely random) or kill X enemies, but also can be way more esoteric or impossible to do if gods of randomness decide against you. The more you progress the harder stage the missions demand, so you'd find yourself going again and again through early stages just to get to the stage where you mission goal might even happen. 

Game gives four characters, each with their own type of weapon, speed, amount of health, amount of dashes and amount of special attacks (glyph, which work in a similarly limited way to dashes and draw on the same random resource pool once exhausted in the fight). You start with Aeon, the balanced option, and subsequently unlock a slow heavy with overheating beam (Big Mo), fragile speedster with rather close range attack (Mukai) and another rather balanced but more advanced option with flamethrower-like blood spray and unique mechanic of using his own health as a currency for updates (Rasimov). Each of the three later characters unlock sequentially as a part of the previous character's permanent unlocks, so good luck grinding missions until you get that far, (especially on Mukai who has a survival potential of wet tissue). Different characters all do have unique abilities which vary their gameplay but I hit plateau around stage 3 and couldn't progress much further, so I cannot say how well or differently they play on later stages. 

(stage environments are a little odd: stage 1 is urban decay streets, stage 2 are labs, stage 3 is some kind of gilded cultic halls and stage 4 is... clowns? why clowns?)

I cannot expect from the game that came way before "Hades" to handle story progression just as well as "Hades" does, so upon unlocking each character you are given a nice cutscene setting them and their backstory up, and then upon completing each stage you get a random (and often repeating) tidbit about them along with a free update from an eyeball man. So instead of the story being a motivator for the unfun and restrictive grind, my only hope is to get to the stage 6 and see if I get any other cutscene. A few more tidbits are given as an epitaph for stages. Even with this little, the world itself is set well – occulto-cyberpunk with at least one secret society – and I do want to know more about it, but going over and over and over through early stages so just to get to the stage where missions might happen and then be screwed by random, by hordes of enemies who are all more and faster and more difficult and (unlike in shmops, don't die in one hit) is definitely not my idea of a good game.

(Rasimov is the only person who looks like he is having fun in all of that). 

Also, when I play more than about 1-2 stages in a row, the game starts to stutter, even on a modern computer, which is, in game, often a death sentence or a lot of health lost for no fault of mine. 

I wish that game to be rescued, rebalanced and reworked. I would dearly love a good CRPG set in that world as I want to know about what happened to Aeon, Big Mo, Mukai and Rasimov. But as it is, I cannot recommend. By this point of time, there are much, much better rogue-likes with much better mechanics and less unfair tedious fruitless grind than "Leap of Fate".

Leap of Fate is a fast and furious roguelite shooter that doesn't try too hard and that's why it works so well for me. The game is not perfect by any means: the UI is very barebones, movements are floaty, mouse crosshair has some annoying lag, most of the graphics are lowpoly models that look like they were lifted off an asset store and the gameplay is nothing new. But it succeeds where many other roguelites have failed, the game is fun enough, and one of the best roguelites I've played.
The full price is a bit high, so buy it on a good sale.
The gameplay is simple, yet will easily deliver more than a dozen hours of good fun in a perfect mix of grind and skill training.
The story is grimdark and there are little comic vignettes that wrap the whole thing nicely. In fact, this game is reminiscent of those edgy low quality comics that were trendy in the 1990s.
I wish more videogames were so self-aware.

Sometimes in life there are budget games that nail a certain type of atmosphere or as ports from the early mobile boom jump the gun of later defined works, but if you lucked out on them at the time of the Apple mobile boom, you might not get what that game meant until many years later.   Or you end up reading msm reviews from game review sites that didn't get what the game was at all.  And no, none of the 

Leap of Fate is one such IOS app port that came over in 2016, it's basically a fanboy's love of the old Mage RPG from the 90's World of Darkness just paired way down  and ported down into a mobile guantlet clone.  Hence the fast paced small themed levels with quick branching cards and a rando mutation stat maker.  And because it IS a mobile port there's a lot of the usual off bits of occasionally wonky hit detection, not a lot of enemy variety.  But for a quick spliff if you get it under 5$ it can be good for a quick spin for an hour or two of fun.

Is this as good as the Hand of Fate Games? No it's not and can't because it's an arcade game with mutators and not a more in depth roguelike.   Just don't get fooled into getting it on full price.

Наишикарнейший рогалик с динамичными боями и необычной смесью магии и киберпанка. У нас есть четыре мага (сначала один, в процессе игры открываются остальные) с разными способностями, целями и стилями игры. Наша цель - пройти через Горнило Судеб, магический полигон для испытаний талантов магов, и узнать свою судьбу.
Горнило представляет собой шесть арен-уровней: городские улицы, секретная лаборатория, башня магов, прошлое, настоящее и будущее (забвение). На каждом из уровней раскладывается рандомная колода с боями, испытаниями, апгрейдами, подарками и пр. Нужно дойти до низа колоды, отыскать карту Хранителя, победить его и перейти на следующий уровень. На каждом уровне свои противники, особенности окружения и тактики.
Бои протекают очень динамично и немного напоминают старую игру "Crimsonland": на нас со всех сторон несутся толпы противников, мы мечемся по карте и уничтожаем их самыми разными способами. В нашем распоряжении: базовая атака (разная у каждого мага), глифы (по одному базовому у каждого мага и около 20 штук приобретаемых, с разнообразным действием, от классического призыва голема или метеоритного дождя до похищения противников инопланетянами), Призрачный Ветер (местный аналог телепортации, при должной раскачке становится грозным оружием), взрывы интерактивного окружения. В общем, всё происходит очень быстро и не расслабляет ни на секунду.
У каждого мага есть перманентные апгрейды, открывающиеся при выполнении мини-заданий в игре и сохраняющиеся на протяжении всего прохождения. Также во время каждого "забега" мы прокачиваем героев рандомно выпадающими способностями (на выбор), изменяющимися от игры к игре. Все они относительно универсальны, но, так как каждый маг имеет предрасположенность к определённому стилю игры (к примеру, у Аэона хорошие бонусы к Призрачному Ветру, а Большой Мо наносит мощный урон базовой атакой), то раскачивать лучше навыки, соответствующие этому стилю. Всего имеется три ветки навыков: "тело" - прокачка урона базовой атаки, автоатаки, дроны, увеличение ёмкости глифа и т.д.; "ноги" - раскачка Призрачного Ветра (поджог, выстрелы, приманки, страх и пр.) и "голова" - манипуляции с колодой, увеличение здоровья и скорости и др.
Для каждого из героев имеется пять абсолютно разных и не связанных друг с другом концовок. Две из них даются за прохождение игры на нормальном и тяжёлом уровнях сложности, другие три открываются при выполнении определённых условий в процессе игры или нескольких игр.
В общем, это прекрасный, динамичный и нескучный рогалик с интересным геймплеем. Однозначно рекомендую.

People. Please. This game is a roguelite as defined in the game description NOT a roguelike or action-roguelike.

It's not too heavy in the roguelite elements but it does require you to replay the game over and over to unlock hard mode and some other features that make the game tremendously easier. And you have to do this separately for every character.

The game is pretty easy and the only difficulty that comes with it is in the worst way possible. Artificial difficulty based on RNG on what skill/glyph you pick up in the game and some questionable game design decisions.

Game has 6 stages. Levels 1-5 is a joke and level 6 suddenly has the most unreasonable game difficulty spike I have seen.

I made it to the last level easily on first run and suddenly was literally one shot by a mob 100 to 0. Was pretty disappointing, but with the unlocked roguelite upgrades I got from this run, the next run I beat normal mode fairly easily. Then I had to beat it 2 more times to unlock hard mode (specifically, completing the missions).

The game is deceptively highly customizable. There are three skill trees that seemingly get randomized every run for each category meaning skills deep in a tree might appear in the early-middle of the tree/path in some runs. The skill card you pick up / unlock in each level randomly gives you a category, then you can pick a skill. 

And the skills just add passive effect bonuses to basically your passive attack or your dash. Essentially, there really isn't much different gameplay you can do.

You shoot. You dash through people. That's it. The special upgrades just improve one of those two things.

There are glyphs which is your limited right click / mana usage. This is the easily worst part of the game and determines whether you easily win a run or have to struggle and play like a god to win.

Some glyphs are trash while some are so OP. 

Imagine one run I pick up a glyph so OP that I walk up to the last boss - spam my limited attack 10 times and effectively kill him in 2 seconds and he doesn't have a chance to do anything. Wow I'm so good at the game. 

Another run, I had such an awful glyph that I spent a good 5-10 minutes running around dodging attacks until I run out of dash charges then I literally can't do anything. The game isn't the type of game where you can dodge everything with just wasd with your giant hit box, slow move speed, and sometimes confined maps with narrow hallways and terrain. The last boss seems to be randomly generated as well from a list of possibilities. If you have a combination of bad glyph, bad map, and unfavorable boss match up you just lose. Good luck avoiding damage on a ranged boss that you have to use a dash to avoid and if you don't do enough DPS, you run out of dashes charges then die.

Hard mode doesn't change anything other than seemingly add some "curses" to some battles making them harder, less hp upgrades, enemies do more damage maybe. My glyph was decent, not OP, but the map was pretty good for what I had and both bosses were melee, so I kited them out easily. Thankfully, I didn't have to play anymore of this terrible game.

Leap of Fate é um roguelike com temática cyberpunk em que magia e tecnologia se confundem em uma coisa só.  O jogo trás quatro personagens com backgrounds distintos, mas que, por uma razão ou outra, são levados a enfrentar o Crisol dos Destinos.

O local é na verdade um campo de provações em que o destino dos participantes é dado de acordo com um deck de cartas, onde apenas sobrevivem aqueles capazes de superar seus próprios medos. 

Na prática isso significa enfrentar hordas de monstros em fases que são compostas por um conjunto de cartas viradas para baixo. O objetivo é encontrar a carta que leva para a próxima rodada, revelando uma por uma de cima para baixo.

No caminho, muitas das cartas são de combate, mas também existem aquelas onde é possível melhorar alguma habilidade, comprar itens na loja ou até receber algum bônus, seja gratuitamente ou através de algum sacrifício de vida.

Porém, a narrativa não se desenvolve bem e é deixada em segundo plano. Não fica claro qual a relação entre as cartas e os personagens ou ainda qual a natureza da criatura misteriosa que os guia. A impressão que passa é que a história foi criada para o Aeon e os outros personagens estão lá só para diversificar a jogatina, sem reais conexões com o enredo.

Inicialmente é mostrado a você o passado de cada um, e conforme você vai avançando com os personagens, vão sendo mostrados seus possíveis destinos. São cinco diferentes para cada um, mas para ver tudo, é necessário finalizar a campanha no modo difícil com todos eles.

Isso não é uma tarefa das mais fáceis, pois o jogo não tolera erros, e qualquer falha pode te forçar a ter que começar tudo novamente, já que o jogo trabalha com a ideia de morte permanente.

Além disso, as fases são geradas de forma aleatória, de acordo com as cartas que você puxa a cada rodada. Assim, seu sucesso depende muito da sua habilidade, mas também exige um pouco de sorte para encontrar as cartas que você está precisando naquele momento.

No combate, é boa a variação de estilo entre os personagens, sendo que cada um conta com um ataque padrão e duas habilidades que podem ser aprimoradas/alteradas no decorrer do jogo com o uso de mana, recurso que aqui funciona como moeda de troca.

Tais alterações só valem pra o jogo atual e serão descartadas caso você morra, mas ao final de cada fase você recebe missões que, uma vez cumpridas, vão melhorar algumas características daquele personagem de forma permanente e possibilitar desbloquear os outros personagens.

Desbloqueei todos, joguei um pouco com cada um deles e vi alguns dos destinos, mas não encontrei motivação para continuar jogando e ver todos os finais. A questão é que não há aquela sensação de progresso, mas pelo contrário, você sente que está preso repetindo as mesmas fases e lutando contra os mesmos inimigos genéricos. 

Em resumo, Leap of Fate tem ideias interessantes, mas que não foram muito bem trabalhadas. Soma-se a isso uma fraca narrativa, e temos um jogo que em pouco tempo se torna cansativo. Embora tenha uma dificuldade mais alta que a média dos jogos atuais, não é nada impossível, mas você simplesmente não terá paciência para persistir jogando. FRACO (5/10).

Responsive controls and a random skill tree on every playthrough. This is not Diablo-like as there's no loot or extensive build-crafting; it is a good twin-stick shooter. The missions are bite sized but they move so fast that you can easily lose an hour trying to complete the next one, with permanent upgrades awarded for completing special objectives.
